sections.overview: The Iceland scallop is a cold-water fan shell of the North Atlantic and Arctic margins. It belongs to the pectinid scallops, alongside the better-known Atlantic sea scallop, but is a distinct subarctic species.
sections.identification: Its rounded fan-shaped shell has radiating ribs and two small ear-like projections beside the hinge; shell colours vary from pale to reddish or brown. Adults can exceed 10 cm in shell height, though size and growth differ among beds.
sections.habitat: It lives on the seabed in cool, shallow subarctic waters, commonly on sand, shell gravel and mixed coarse bottoms. Around Iceland, major beds are concentrated in fjords, often between about 15 and 75 m deep.
sections.diet: Like other scallops, it filter-feeds: gills retain suspended microscopic food, especially phytoplankton and organic particles. Seasonal food supply helps explain why growth changes through the year.
sections.behavior: It can clap its valves and jet water to swim briefly away from disturbance, although adults usually remain on the bottom.
sections.reproduction: The sexes release eggs and sperm into the water, where fertilisation occurs; larvae then drift before settling. Its slow growth means that a fishery cannot quickly replace lost adults.
sections.ecology: Scallop beds support attached organisms and provide prey for bottom-feeding predators such as starfish. The species’ cold-water range overlaps with other pectinids, but its life history and stock trends should not be assumed to match those of the Atlantic sea scallop.
sections.conservation: Icelandic stocks collapsed around 1999–2000, and a zero quota was advised in 2004; overfishing, a protozoan disease and warmer bottom water were implicated. This is a historical, stock-specific fishery record, not a current global threatened-species category.
